channel.title: PsyDigest — psychiatry literature digest
channel.description: Summaries of new psychiatric research and guidelines

item.title: [29] Digital Therapeutic Interventions for Suicide Prevention: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Their Effectiveness in Reducing Suicidal Ideation and Suicide Attempts.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study addresses whether digital therapeutic interventions (e.g., apps, online programs) reduce suicidal ideation or suicide attempts in randomized clinical trials (RCTs). It synthesizes 17 RCTs (N = 5,089) to clarify mixed prior findings and assess durability of effects.
FINDINGS: Digital interventions significantly reduced suicidal ideation immediately (Hedges’ g = –0.61, 95 % CI not reported) and at follow-up (g = –0.77). The relative risk of suicide attempts was reduced (RR ≈ 0.7–0.8) but not statistically significant. Effects were larger in clinical populations, self-guided formats, and younger participants; heterogeneity was high (I² not reported).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is moderate-sized but heterogeneous, with potential risk of bias across diverse digital formats and control conditions. The statistically significant reduction in suicidal ideation is of uncertain clinical magnitude; the non-significant trend for fewer attempts precludes firm conclusions. Publication bias assessment was limited and funding sources were not disclosed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Digital interventions may offer a useful adjunct for reducing suicidal thoughts, especially in younger or clinical subgroups, but current evidence does not yet justify replacing standard care for suicide prevention. Clinicians should monitor emerging high-quality RCTs before integrating these tools routinely.

item.title: [15] Learning from neurodivergent students about their mental health and wellbeing during transition to secondary school: A systematic review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study addresses how the transition from primary to secondary school affects mental health and wellbeing in neurodivergent children (e.g., autistic youth, those with developmental language disorder, or Down syndrome), using a neurodiversity-informed framework. It is a systematic review of longitudinal empirical studies with child-reported outcomes, aiming to clarify inconsistent findings in this emerging research area.
FINDINGS: Out of 488 records screened, only 10 studies met inclusion criteria, all longitudinal with comparison groups and at least two timepoints around the school transition. Due to substantial heterogeneity, a narrative synthesis was conducted. Findings on mental health outcomes were mixed and inconclusive, but psychosocial factors—such as school belonging and connectedness—showed more consistent vulnerability signals. Key gaps included lack of participatory research, underrepresentation of certain neurodivergent groups, and limited attention to intersectional factors like ethnicity and socioeconomic status.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is very limited and heterogeneous, with no meta-analysis possible. The reliance on narrative synthesis and small, varied samples reduces confidence in any firm conclusions. The stronger signal in psychosocial outcomes suggests these may be more sensitive indicators than mental health symptoms, but causality and clinical significance remain unclear. The absence of co-produced research and intersectional analyses limits generalisability and clinical applicability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not support specific clinical recommendations for managing mental health during school transition in neurodivergent youth. Clinicians should prioritise monitoring psychosocial adjustment (e.g., belonging, school concerns) rather than assuming uniform mental health deterioration. Future practice should await more rigorous, participatory, and intersectionally informed research before implementing targeted interventions.

item.title: [12] Metabolic syndrome in stable long-term antipsychotic monotherapy and polypharmacy among patients with schizophrenia: a real-world comparative study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This retrospective cohort study in a Swedish community mental health centre asked whether antipsychotic polypharmacy, compared with monotherapy, is independently associated with metabolic syndrome in adults with schizophrenia who had been on a stable regimen for ≥5 years. 370 patients were included.
FINDINGS: Metabolic syndrome was present in 38.6 % overall (41.2 % polypharmacy vs 34.7 % monotherapy, p = 0.216). Polypharmacy patients had higher chlorpromazine-equivalent doses (median 1010 vs 454.5 mg/day, p < 0.001) and more LAI use (67.3 % vs 37.5 %, p < 0.001). In multivariable logistic regression, neither polypharmacy (adjusted OR 1.220, 95 % CI 0.767–1.941, p = 0.401), daily dose increments of 100 mg (adjusted OR 1.003, 95 % CI 0.954–1.055, p = 0.899), nor LAI use were independently linked to metabolic syndrome. Current smoking showed the only independent association (adjusted OR 1.996, 95 % CI 1.251–3.185, p = 0.004).
INTERPRETATION: The study’s retrospective design and selection of long-term stable patients limit causal inference; residual confounding (e.g., illness severity, prior treatments) cannot be excluded. The confidence intervals around the null associations are wide, so clinically meaningful effects cannot be ruled out. The clearest modifiable risk factor was smoking, underscoring the need for cardiometabolic monitoring and smoking cessation interventions regardless of regimen.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For patients on long-term antipsychotic treatment, switching from polypharmacy to monotherapy primarily to reduce metabolic risk is not supported by these data. Focus should remain on routine metabolic screening and smoking cessation rather than regimen simplification per se.

item.title: [11] Peripartum Esketamine: A Narrative Review of Analgesia, Postpartum Depressive Symptoms, Sleep-Related Outcomes, and Safety.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines whether peripartum esketamine can improve pain control, reduce postpartum depressive symptoms, enhance sleep, and maintain maternal-infant safety. It synthesizes mechanistic rationale and clinical studies, primarily single-center trials in cesarean-delivery populations.
FINDINGS: Short-term analgesic benefit is consistently reported, but opioid-sparing effects are inconsistent. Several RCTs suggest low-dose peri-delivery esketamine may lower early Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) screening positives, though diagnostic outcomes are sparse. Sleep benefits are preliminary and based on subjective measures. Maternal and neonatal tolerability appear acceptable in the short term, but pregnancy pharmacokinetics, lactation data, and long-term offspring neurodevelopment remain insufficiently studied.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited by study design heterogeneity, small single-center samples, and reliance on screening tools rather than diagnostic interviews. Strengths include consistent short-term analgesic findings and signals for mood improvement, but the lack of objective sleep measures, standardized dosing, and long-term safety data constrains confidence. The clinical significance of observed mood effects is uncertain given the absence of diagnostic confirmation and long-term follow-up.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Esketamine may be considered as an individualized adjunct for peripartum pain management, but routine prophylactic use for mood or sleep is not supported by current evidence. Clinicians should await larger multicenter trials with diagnostic outcomes and long-term safety assessments before changing practice.

item.title: [10] Feasibility and Acceptability of Videoconference-Based Family Psychoeducation for Young Adult Caregivers of Family Members With Major Depressive Disorder: Protocol for a Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is a protocol for a waitlist-controlled pilot randomized controlled trial (RCT) examining the feasibility and acceptability of videoconference-based family psychoeducation (vFPE) for young adult caregivers (aged 18–39) of family members with major depressive disorder (MDD). The study addresses a gap in support programs for this vulnerable group, who face psychological distress and caregiving burdens during a critical developmental period.
FINDINGS: The protocol outlines a 1:1 randomized trial with 4 weekly 40-minute vFPE sessions. Primary outcomes are feasibility (recruitment, randomization, completion, dropout, safety) and acceptability (Client Satisfaction Questionnaire-8). Exploratory outcomes (e.g., anxiety, depression, caregiver burden) will be assessed at baseline, postintervention, and 1-month follow-up. As of May 2026, 8 participants had been enrolled, with recruitment and data collection ongoing until March 2028.
INTERPRETATION: This is a feasibility study, not designed to test efficacy. Strengths include its randomized design and focus on a neglected population, but conclusions are premature given the small sample size and ongoing recruitment. The protocol’s rigor depends on adherence to randomization and blinding (if any), but no effect sizes or preliminary results are yet available. External validity is uncertain until feasibility metrics (e.g., dropout rates, satisfaction) are reported.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No clinical conclusions can be drawn yet. If feasibility is demonstrated, this could pave the way for a larger RCT to assess effectiveness. Clinicians should monitor future results to determine whether vFPE is a viable option for young adult caregivers in routine care.

item.title: [10] A Typology of Moderator Practices and Community Guidelines in Online Mental Health Communities to Establish a Framework for Digital Safety: Systematized Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Online mental health communities (OMHCs) provide peer support but face challenges in ensuring safety and supportive interactions through moderation practices and community guidelines. This systematized review aimed to develop typologies of moderator practices and guideline content in OMHCs for people with mental health problems, synthesizing empirical and gray literature from 2014 to 2024.
FINDINGS: The review included 80 documents (48 empirical papers and 32 gray literature) covering 52 OMHCs. Four categories of moderator practices were identified: (1) premoderation/postmoderation processes (used in 79% of OMHCs), (2) reactive moderation, (3) community-building, and (4) member monitoring. Three categories of community guideline content emerged: (1) content of posts (used in 67% of OMHCs), (2) member conduct, and (3) moderation. Thematic analysis synthesized these findings into a structured framework.
INTERPRETATION: This systematized review provides a structured framework for moderator practices and guideline content in OMHCs, addressing a critical gap in digital safety. Strengths include the broad inclusion of empirical and gray literature and the development of actionable typologies. However, as a systematized review (not a full systematic review), it lacks formal risk-of-bias assessment and may overrepresent certain OMHCs. The findings are descriptive and lack quantitative effect sizes or comparative data. External validity depends on the diversity of OMHCs included, which may not fully represent all platforms or cultural contexts.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This framework could guide the development of moderator training, digital tools, and governance policies in OMHCs, potentially improving safety and support for users. Clinicians should be aware of these typologies when recommending or evaluating OMHCs, but further research is needed to assess their impact on user outcomes and safety.

item.title: [9] Altered GABAB receptor sensitivity in heavy drinkers indexed using a TMS-based biomarker: a randomized controlled experimental medicine trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study tested whether heavy alcohol use alters sensitivity of metabotropic GABAB receptors (GABABRs) using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) biomarkers and a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover design in 31 healthy volunteers (16 heavy drinkers, 15 light drinkers).
FINDINGS: Baclofen 30 mg and 60 mg produced dose-dependent increases in growth hormone (GH) release, confirming central GABABR engagement. Long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI) increased after baclofen in light drinkers at both doses, suggesting a plateau effect. In heavy drinkers, LICI increased at 30 mg but not at 60 mg despite similar drug levels, indicating altered GABABR sensitivity under higher agonist stimulation.
INTERPRETATION: The randomized crossover design and biomarker confirmation strengthen internal validity. The small sample and healthy volunteer population limit generalizability to clinical AUD. The differential LICI response at higher dose suggests altered receptor function in heavy drinkers, but clinical significance remains uncertain without outcome data.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Findings support further investigation of TMS-based biomarkers for GABABR target engagement but do not yet justify changes in AUD treatment. Watch for emerging studies linking these biomarkers to clinical outcomes.

item.title: [9] Exercise as a complementary intervention for adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a neurobiological analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review explores potential neurobiological mechanisms by which physical exercise could alleviate symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity in adults with ADHD, where evidence for exercise as a treatment is limited compared to children.
FINDINGS: The review synthesizes mechanistic hypotheses—including enhanced neuroplasticity, improved functional brain connectivity, neurotransmitter modulation, and reduced neuroinflammation—based on heterogeneous, largely observational data and indirect evidence from non-ADHD populations. No clinical outcome data or effect sizes are reported.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is preliminary and methodologically weak: reliance on a single database, single-author screening, and lack of direct adult ADHD intervention studies limit internal validity. The proposed mechanisms are biologically plausible but remain unconfirmed in the target population. External validity is uncertain due to indirect data sources.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Exercise may hold promise as a low-cost, accessible adjunct for adults with ADHD, but current evidence is insufficient to recommend it as a treatment. Clinicians should view exercise as supportive care while awaiting rigorous trials to confirm efficacy and clarify mechanisms.

item.title: [9] Design, reporting, and research focus of neurology and psychiatry drug trials (2020-2023): a registry-based meta-epidemiological study using ClinicalTrials.gov and NLP.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This registry-based meta-epidemiological study used ClinicalTrials.gov data (2000–2023) with NLP and manual validation to quantify design features, reporting practices, and research focus in neurology and psychiatry drug trials. The clinical question concerns how these trials are conducted and reported, which affects evidence synthesis and future trial planning.
FINDINGS: Among 18,609 trials, most were early-phase (60% completed), single-center, and small (median 11–50 participants). Industry funded 36%, declining over time; university sponsorship increased. Ten percent were non-randomized and 38% open-label. Among trials completed after 2007, only 50% reported results, with a mean delay of 12 months. Top conditions studied were pain (10%), schizophrenia (8%), depression (8%), and Alzheimer’s disease (7%). Atypical antipsychotics, levodopa, and ketamine each accounted for 1–2% of trials.
INTERPRETATION: The study highlights persistent deficiencies in trial design (small size, high proportion of non-randomized/open-label trials) and poor results reporting (only half reported results, often delayed). While the large sample size and use of NLP strengthen internal validity, reliance on registry data and lack of clinical outcome assessment limit external validity. The findings suggest a need for improved adherence to reporting standards and better trial design to enhance evidence quality.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should be cautious when interpreting underpowered, open-label, or industry-funded trials in neurology and psychiatry. Improved trial registration and results reporting are essential for evidence-based practice.

item.title: [7] Extended reality as an assistive technology for mental health and wellbeing: a scoping review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This scoping review asks whether Extended Reality (XR—virtual, augmented, and mixed reality) can meaningfully advance mental-health care across conditions such as anxiety, depression, PTSD, ADHD, and autism, given persistent barriers to conventional treatments. Using PRISMA-ScR methods, 277 empirical studies published January 2022–March 2025 were synthesised thematically.
FINDINGS: XR applications spanned anxiety/stress (most frequently studied), depression/mood disorders, PTSD, neurodevelopmental conditions, social isolation, cognitive decline, and workplace stress. Reported benefits were predominantly short-term or preliminary, especially for anxiety and PTSD. Design approaches included immersive exposure, mindfulness/relaxation, social interaction, cognitive stimulation, biofeedback, haptics, and adaptive personalisation. Key constraints were limited longitudinal and comparative evidence, high costs, accessibility barriers, clinician training needs, and ethical/privacy/regulatory concerns.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is preliminary and heterogeneous; most studies are small, short-term, and lack robust comparators. While XR shows promise—particularly for anxiety and PTSD—there is insufficient high-quality evidence to establish sustained clinical impact or cost-effectiveness. Stronger randomised trials with longer follow-up, pragmatic comparisons to usual care, and attention to equity, training, and regulation are needed before widespread adoption.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, XR should be considered experimental for routine psychiatric care; clinicians may cautiously explore XR tools in anxiety/PTSD within research or highly supervised settings, but should not yet adopt them as standard interventions.

item.title: [21] Bipolar Disorder and the Risk of Cardiovascular Diseases: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Observational Studies.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO registered) quantified the prevalence and incidence of cardiovascular diseases (CVD) in adults with bipolar disorder (BD) using observational studies, addressing a key gap in understanding premature mortality risk in this population.
FINDINGS: The pooled CVD prevalence in BD was 7.70% (95% CI: 5.07–11.52), with coronary artery disease at 6.89% (95% CI: 4.05–11.47), cerebrovascular disease at 4.45% (95% CI: 2.13–9.05), and peripheral arterial disease at 3.30% (95% CI: 1.66–6.45). In controlled incidence studies, BD was associated with a 66% higher CVD incidence (IRR 1.66, 95% CI: 1.32–2.08), including elevated risks for coronary and cerebrovascular events.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is limited by extreme heterogeneity in prevalence estimates, reliance on observational designs, and insufficient data on moderators (e.g., medication, lifestyle, comorbidities). While the increased CVD incidence in BD is statistically robust, the pooled estimates are imprecise and not generalizable to specific populations. The lack of adjustment for confounders and noncomparable reporting further weakens causal inference.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The findings support routine cardiovascular screening in adults with BD, but the magnitude and drivers of risk remain uncertain. Clinicians should monitor cardiometabolic health closely, but should not assume precise risk estimates based on these pooled data. Further prospective studies with standardized reporting are needed.

item.title: [19] Efficacy and safety of non-hormonal pharmacotherapies for depressive and anxiety symptoms during the menopausal transition and postmenopause: a systematic review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examined the efficacy and safety of non-hormonal drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, gabapentinoids, etc.) for depressive and anxiety symptoms in peri- and postmenopausal women, synthesizing heterogeneous randomized and non-randomized studies.
FINDINGS: Thirty-one studies (n = 8,124) were included. SNRIs showed more frequent positive effects on depressive symptoms than other classes, while SSRIs had modest and variable effects. Gabapentinoids improved vasomotor symptoms but had limited, low-certainty effects on mood. Anxiety outcomes were inconsistent across all classes. Overall certainty of evidence was very low to moderate.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited by clinical and methodological heterogeneity, indirect comparisons, and lack of head-to-head trials, reducing confidence in conclusions. SNRIs may offer the most consistent benefit for depressive symptoms, but effect sizes and certainty remain uncertain. Anxiety outcomes remain insufficiently supported.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence supports cautious consideration of SNRIs for depressive symptoms in menopausal women, but high-quality comparative trials are needed before firm treatment recommendations can be made.

item.title: [17] Implementation strategies used in clinical practice guidelines in older adults' mental health and neurocognitive conditions: a scoping review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) aim to improve care for older adults with mental health and neurocognitive conditions, but their implementation in practice remains challenging. This scoping review systematically mapped evidence on implementation strategies for CPGs in this population using the JBI methods and EPOC framework.
FINDINGS: Only three peer-reviewed studies were identified. Reported strategies included provider-tailored education and interdisciplinary collaboration. Barriers to implementation included lengthy CPGs, weak evidence perception, and provider doubts about patient relevance. The review highlights a significant gap in the literature.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is extremely limited (n=3 studies), precluding robust conclusions. The review’s strength lies in its systematic mapping, but the paucity of studies and lack of quantitative outcomes undermine internal validity. External validity is unclear due to heterogeneity and unclear generalisability. The findings are preliminary and highlight a critical research gap rather than actionable evidence.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No direct clinical recommendations can be made from this review. It underscores the need for rigorous studies evaluating effective implementation strategies for CPGs in older adult mental health care. Clinicians should remain cautious about relying on untested strategies.

item.title: [10] Association between clozapine-induced hypertriglyceridemia and defenestration of liver sinusoidal endothelial cells.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic but causes severe metabolic side effects, possibly via liver sinusoidal endothelial cell (LSEC) dysfunction. This translational study combined in vitro murine LSEC porosity assays with human serum analyses to test whether clozapine exposure reduces LSEC porosity and correlates with hypertriglyceridemia and hyperglycemia.
FINDINGS: In 72 routine blood samples from clozapine-treated patients, serum clozapine concentration correlated with triglycerides (Spearman’s ρ = 0.47, P = 0.00024) and glucose (ρ = 0.24, P = 0.034), but not with LDL (ρ = –0.04, P = 0.82) or HDL (ρ = –0.22, P = 0.088). In vitro, clozapine caused a concentration-dependent reduction in murine LSEC porosity (P for trend = 0.00036).
INTERPRETATION: The study provides preliminary mechanistic and correlational evidence linking clozapine to LSEC defenestration and metabolic derangements. The human data are observational and cross-sectional, so causality cannot be inferred. The in vitro findings are robust but in a non-human system. Effect sizes are moderate for triglycerides and small for glucose; clinical significance remains uncertain until prospective human data confirm whether LSEC changes precede or merely reflect metabolic disturbances.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings suggest a potential therapeutic target (LSEC porosity) to mitigate clozapine’s metabolic toxicity, but they do not yet change routine monitoring or clozapine prescribing practices. Watch for future interventional studies targeting LSEC function in clozapine-treated patients.

item.title: [6] Two distinct projection pathways converge onto the same BLA neurons to contribute to fear memory retrieval.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This preclinical study in mice examined whether projection pathways from the postrhinal cortex (POR) to the basolateral amygdala (BLA) contribute to context-induced fear memory retrieval, alongside previously identified ventral hippocampus CA1 (vCA1)-BLA projections. The work aims to clarify neural circuit mechanisms relevant to PTSD relapse prevention.
FINDINGS: The authors report that optogenetic manipulation of POR-BLA neurons modulates context-induced fear memory retrieval in mice. They further show that both POR-BLA and vCA1-BLA pathways converge onto the same BLA neurons, suggesting coordinated involvement in fear memory expression. No quantitative effect sizes, confidence intervals, or p-values are provided in the abstract.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and based on animal neurocircuitry research with limited methodological detail in the abstract. While the convergence of two distinct pathways onto common BLA neurons is a plausible mechanism for fear memory retrieval, the clinical relevance remains uncertain. The study lacks human data, effect sizes, and statistical reporting, so the strength of the conclusion cannot be assessed. Further replication and translational studies are needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study does not yet change clinical practice. It offers a mechanistic hypothesis about fear memory circuits that may guide future translational research, but direct implications for PTSD treatment or patient care are not established.

item.title: [6] Network localization of brain structural and functional alterations induced by electroconvulsive therapy for depression.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study aimed to clarify how electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) alters brain structure and function in depression by synthesizing neuroimaging findings and mapping them onto large-scale brain networks. It combined data from 34 published studies (15 structural and 19 functional MRI studies) with connectome datasets to identify ECT-modulated networks.
FINDINGS: The analysis identified distinct ECT-modulated structural and functional networks. The structural network primarily involved subcortical regions (hippocampus, amygdala), ventral attention areas (insula, operculum, temporoparietal junction), and somatomotor regions (precentral and postcentral gyrus). The functional network mainly implicated the default mode network (medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex).
INTERPRETATION: This is a meta-analytic and network-mapping study, not a primary clinical trial, so causal inferences about ECT’s antidepressant effects cannot be drawn. The strength lies in integrating heterogeneous neuroimaging data to propose a network-level mechanism, but the clinical relevance of these structural/functional changes remains uncertain. The dissociation between structural and functional networks is intriguing but preliminary; replication in larger, longitudinal cohorts with clinical outcome data is needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study suggests ECT may exert its antidepressant effects through network-specific brain changes, but it does not yet inform treatment decisions. Clinicians should note that ECT’s mechanisms likely involve distributed brain networks rather than isolated regions, but this remains a research finding until linked to patient outcomes.

item.title: [19] Acceptability and Experience of Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Adult ADHD: A Systematic Review With Narrative Synthesis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review with narrative synthesis examined the acceptability of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) for adults with ADHD, addressing a gap in understanding how core ADHD symptoms may influence treatment engagement and satisfaction. The review included 21 studies (RCTs, pilot/feasibility trials, qualitative and mixed-methods studies) and mapped findings to the seven domains of the Theoretical Framework of Acceptability (TFA).
FINDINGS: Acceptability was most consistently assessed in the domains of affective attitude, intervention coherence, perceived effectiveness, and self-efficacy. Positive drivers included skills training, psychoeducation, therapeutic support, accountability strategies, and individualisation. Burden was primarily associated with homework demands, cognitive load, and treatment intensity. Group and digital formats were generally acceptable but depended on facilitation quality, accessibility, and therapeutic presence. Ethicality and opportunity costs were rarely reported.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is heterogeneous, combining diverse study designs and measures, which limits firm conclusions. However, the synthesis suggests that CBT for adult ADHD is most acceptable when it enhances engagement, understanding, and perceived benefit while minimising burden. The review highlights the importance of intervention content and delivery style over format alone. Key limitations include the lack of standardised acceptability measures and underreporting of ethical and opportunity-cost domains.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should prioritise structured, flexible CBT interventions that incorporate psychoeducation, skills training, and accountability strategies to improve acceptability. Attention to homework load and cognitive demands may reduce treatment burden. Further research using standardised acceptability measures is needed to refine delivery approaches.

item.title: [16] Outcomes of Mindful Mood Balance for Moms, online mindfulness-based cognitive therapy for perinatal depressive relapse prevention in the USA: a two-arm, single-blind, pragmatic randomised clinical trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study evaluated whether adding an online mindfulness-based cognitive therapy programme (Mindful Mood Balance for Moms) to usual care reduces depressive relapse and symptom burden in euthymic pregnant women with recurrent depression in the USA, using a two-arm, single-blind, pragmatic RCT.
FINDINGS: In 500 participants (mean age 32 years, mean 11.5 weeks gestation), MMB for Moms reduced relapse risk over 6 months postpartum (33% vs 44%; hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.56–0.99; p=0.045). Symptom burden decreased more during the 12-week intervention (average PHQ-9 reduction 0.75 vs 0.31), but not across the full trial period (0.61 vs 0.54).
INTERPRETATION: The trial suggests a modest reduction in relapse risk and short-term symptom improvement with MMB for Moms versus usual care. Strengths include pragmatic design and low attrition (77–78% follow-up). However, the effect on relapse is modest (HR ~0.74), the CI approaches 1, and symptom benefits did not persist postpartum. Funding from NIH/NIMH supports credibility, but generalisability to non-academic settings or outside the USA is uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: MMB for Moms may offer a non-pharmacological adjunct for perinatal relapse prevention, particularly during pregnancy, but the clinical impact appears limited and not sustained postpartum; integration should be cautious pending replication and cost-effectiveness data.

item.title: [15] Effects of EEG neurofeedback in adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review of randomised and non-randomised studies.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examined whether EEG neurofeedback improves symptoms, cognition, or brain activity in adults with ADHD, comparing standard and personalised training protocols. Seven studies (three RCTs, four non-randomised; n = 390) were included.
FINDINGS: RCTs showed small, generally non-significant effects on ADHD symptoms versus controls (effect sizes not reported). Non-randomised studies reported larger symptom reductions, but with high risk of bias. Cognitive gains were inconsistent and likely due to practice effects. Protocol-specific EEG changes were observed without convergence across studies. No treatment-related adverse events were reported.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited by small samples, heterogeneous protocols, variable controls, and risk of bias. RCTs do not currently support efficacy over placebo. Non-randomised studies suggest potential benefit but are prone to confounding. High-quality, blinded RCTs with standardised outcome measures are needed to determine clinical utility.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: EEG neurofeedback cannot be recommended as an evidence-based treatment for adult ADHD based on current data. Clinicians should discuss this uncertainty with patients and consider established treatments while awaiting better trials.

item.title: [12] Undertreatment of Wernicke encephalopathy in alcohol-related clinical contexts: a scoping review of diagnosis, thiamine regimens, and clinical management.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Wernicke encephalopathy (WE) is a preventable neurological emergency in alcohol use disorder (AUD) that is often missed or undertreated due to diagnostic uncertainty and heterogeneous management. This scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) mapped evidence on diagnosis and thiamine regimens in AUD or clinically significant alcohol use, focusing on practice variability and undertreatment.
FINDINGS: Only 26 studies were included, with only two RCTs on thiamine regimens; no consensus on optimal dosing emerged. Diagnostic criteria varied widely, and observational studies consistently reported undertreatment, including delayed initiation and frequent use of oral thiamine in high-risk scenarios. Protocolized, guideline-concordant care was associated with earlier parenteral thiamine use in suspected/confirmed WE.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited, heterogeneous, and underpowered, with no clear optimal thiamine regimen. While diagnostic variability and undertreatment are well-documented, the strength of conclusions is constrained by the lack of high-quality trials and inconsistent diagnostic criteria. Early recognition and parenteral thiamine in high-risk cases remain plausible but unproven strategies to reduce morbidity.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should prioritize early suspicion of WE in AUD patients, use parenteral thiamine in high-risk cases, and follow local protocols where available, while acknowledging the lack of definitive evidence for optimal dosing or regimen.

item.title: [11] Protocol for a parallel-group superiority randomized controlled trial comparing Sage- a couple psychotherapy- to supportive individual psychotherapy for borderline personality disorder.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) carries high mortality and morbidity, and frontline treatments are often inaccessible or only partially effective. Sage is a novel, protocolized couple psychotherapy for BPD that targets both patient symptoms and relationship conflict, but its superiority over standard supportive care has not yet been tested in a rigorous trial. This is a single-blind, parallel-group RCT protocol comparing Sage to supportive individual psychotherapy in 152 couples where one partner has BPD.
FINDINGS: The trial randomizes couples to 16 weeks of Sage (couple-based) versus supportive individual psychotherapy (separate sessions for patient and partner). Primary outcome is BPD symptom change; secondary outcomes include relationship conflict and partner mental health. Assessments occur at baseline, mid-treatment, post-treatment, and 1-, 3-, and 6-month follow-ups. Primary analysis will use intent-to-treat generalized mixed linear models. No results are reported yet.
INTERPRETATION: This is a well-designed, adequately powered RCT with masked assessors and independent supervision to prevent drift, which strengthens internal validity. However, as a protocol paper, no outcome data are available, so efficacy, effect sizes, and safety remain unknown. The design addresses an important gap—testing whether adding a relationship-focused component improves outcomes—but generalizability may be limited by the requirement of a stable intimate partner and the exclusion of individuals without one.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Until results are published, clinicians should view Sage as an experimental intervention. Standard evidence-based treatments for BPD (e.g., DBT, MBT) remain first-line while this trial is ongoing.

item.title: [10] [Efficacy and tolerability of co-administration of clozapine with atypical antipsychotics in patients with treatment-resistant schizophrenia, comorbid with chemical addictions].
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study compared six clozapine-plus-atypical-antipsychotic combinations in 470 adults with treatment-resistant paranoid schizophrenia, 83 % of whom also had a comorbid substance use disorder. It is a six-arm, open-label RCT conducted across multiple Russian psychiatric centres (2018–2026).
FINDINGS: After 42 days, combinations with cariprazine and, to a lesser extent, lurasidone produced significantly greater reductions in positive and negative symptoms than the other four regimens (p < 0.05). The cariprazine group also had the longest subsequent outpatient treatment duration. No adverse events were attributed to the combinations.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and of low internal validity: randomisation method and allocation concealment are not described, raters were unblinded, and no adverse-event monitoring protocol is mentioned. The 42-day horizon is short for a chronic disorder, and the lack of placebo or clozapine-monotherapy arms precludes firm conclusions about incremental benefit. Effect sizes and confidence intervals are not reported, so statistical versus clinical significance cannot be judged.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings do not yet justify changing practice. Clozapine plus cariprazine may be considered on a case-by-case basis when negative symptoms dominate, but clinicians should await larger, longer, and better-controlled trials before adopting this strategy routinely.

item.title: [10] Complex post-traumatic stress disorder in refugees, asylum seekers, and internally displaced people: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis quantified the prevalence of complex post-traumatic stress disorder (CPTSD) in forcibly displaced populations (refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced people) and assessed whether CPTSD adds clinically meaningful information beyond classic PTSD in this group. Twenty studies (17 independent samples, n = 12,504) were synthesised.
FINDINGS: Pooled CPTSD prevalence was 20.9 % (95 % CI 12.6–32.6 %), but heterogeneity was extreme (I² = 98.3 %; 95 % prediction interval 1.7–80.3 %). Prevalence was 10.6 % in community samples versus 55.2 % in treatment-seeking samples. Asylum seekers showed higher rates than refugees. Across four studies, post-migration living difficulties correlated more strongly with disturbances in self-organisation (DSO) than with core PTSD symptoms.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is large but highly heterogeneous and geographically uneven. The pooled estimate should be treated as a descriptive summary rather than a generalisable prevalence. The stronger link between ongoing adversity and DSO supports the clinical relevance of the CPTSD construct in displaced populations, but causal inferences are limited by cross-sectional designs and inconsistent reporting of confounders.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: CPTSD appears common in forcibly displaced people, especially among asylum seekers and those seeking care, suggesting routine screening and trauma-focused interventions are warranted; however, local prevalence may vary widely, so services should adapt to local post-migration stressors rather than rely on a single global estimate.

item.title: [10] Caution before canonisation: a clinical and implementation science perspective on psychedelics.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review critically appraises the emerging evidence for psychedelic-assisted therapies (e.g., psilocybin, MDMA) in psychiatry, focusing on their therapeutic promise and methodological limitations. It synthesizes early clinical trials across depression, PTSD, and substance use disorders to assess readiness for routine care.
FINDINGS: Early trials report rapid symptom improvements under controlled conditions, but many suffer from small sample sizes (often <50 per arm), short follow-up (weeks to months), functional unblinding (due to psychoactive effects), and inconsistent safety reporting. The evidence base is preliminary, heterogeneous, and lacks comparative effectiveness against established treatments.
INTERPRETATION: The review highlights proof-of-concept efficacy but emphasizes major translational gaps: durability of effects, standardized safety protocols, and real-world feasibility. The lack of robust, long-term data and methodological rigor limits causal inference and generalizability. Ethical and implementation challenges (e.g., training, access) further complicate adoption. The findings are promising but not yet definitive.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Psychedelic therapies remain experimental; clinicians should await larger, longer, and methodologically rigorous trials before considering integration into routine care. Current evidence supports continued research but not routine use outside specialized settings.

item.title: [9] A combined study of whole-exome sequencing and structural neuroimaging markers in bipolar disorder.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study explores whether rare genetic variants identified via whole-exome sequencing (WES) in patients with bipolar disorder (BD) are associated with structural brain changes, addressing a gap in understanding the genetic underpinnings of BD using neuroimaging-genetic association analysis.
FINDINGS: WES was conducted on 93 BD patients and 161 healthy controls (HCs). The study identified 382 BD-related genes, including SYNE1, PKHD1L1, FRAS1, and ZFHX4, and highlighted a novel gene, GNB3, with a significant burden of rare nonsynonymous variants linked to BD. Additionally, the SNP rs56850341 in KMT2C was found to be substantially correlated with cortical thickness and white matter tract integrity in BD patients.
INTERPRETATION: This is a small, exploratory case-control study combining WES with neuroimaging, which limits generalizability and causal inference. The findings suggest potential genetic contributors to BD and brain structural changes, but the sample size is modest, and the associations require replication in larger, longitudinal cohorts. The clinical significance of these genetic variants remains uncertain without further functional validation or larger-scale studies.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Currently, these findings do not directly inform clinical practice, as the genetic variants identified are not actionable for diagnosis or treatment. Further research is needed to determine if these associations are reproducible and clinically meaningful.

item.title: [7] A novel digital hybrid care model for maternal mental health: preliminary findings from a matched retrospective cohort study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Peripartum mood and anxiety disorders are common but often undertreated due to access barriers. This matched retrospective cohort study evaluated a hybrid digital care model (Digital Clinic) combining clinician-delivered CBT with app-based support for peripartum women with anxiety/depression.
FINDINGS: The peripartum cohort (n=13) showed a large reduction in GAD-7 scores from 14.4 (SD 5.0) to 5.5 (SD 4.3), mean change −8.9 points (p < 0.01; d = −1.91, 95% CI −2.89 to −0.93). PHQ-9 scores fell from 9.3 (SD 5.9) to 5.6 (SD 4.8), mean change −3.7 points (p = 0.055; d = −0.68, 95% CI −1.41 to 0.05).
INTERPRETATION: The study’s retrospective design, small peripartum sample, and lack of a concurrent control group limit causal inference. The large anxiety effect is statistically robust but based on a tiny cohort; depressive symptom change was not statistically significant. Funding sources and blinding status were not reported, raising potential bias risks. Larger, adequately powered RCTs are needed to confirm effectiveness and generalisability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These preliminary findings suggest a hybrid digital model may reduce anxiety symptoms in peripartum women, but current evidence is insufficient to change routine practice; further rigorous trials are required before recommending widespread adoption.

item.title: [6] Clinical and genetic correlates of a circadian subtype of depression in the Australian Genetics of Depression Study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional study from the Australian Genetics of Depression Study examined whether a circadian subtype of depression—defined by ≥3 circadian features—differs clinically, pharmacologically, and genetically from non-circadian depression in 2604 adults (80% female, mean age 37.9 years).
FINDINGS: The circadian subtype (23% of participants) showed earlier onset (P<0.001), more severe symptoms (including suicidality and psychotic-like experiences, P<0.001), greater weight gain during episodes (P<0.001), and poorer self-reported response to SSRIs (OR 0.88 [95% CI 0.82–0.94]) and SNRIs (OR 0.89 [95% CI 0.83–0.97]). It was associated with higher polygenic risk for ADHD, depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, metabolic traits, inflammatory markers, and later chronotype (all P<0.05).
INTERPRETATION: The study’s cross-sectional design and self-reported outcomes limit causal inference. Selection bias (female-predominant, online-recruited sample) and lack of clinician-rated outcomes reduce external validity. The small effect sizes (ORs ~0.88–1.15) suggest limited clinical predictiveness at present. Genetic associations are hypothesis-generating and require replication.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No immediate treatment change is warranted; the circadian subtype may flag higher symptom burden and lower SSRI/SNRI response, but evidence is preliminary. Future longitudinal studies with objective measures and clinician-rated outcomes are needed before considering tailored interventions.

item.title: [6] From Protective Factors to Mechanisms: Charting the Neurobiology of Schizophrenia Resilience.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review explores neurobiological and psychological mechanisms that may promote resilience to schizophrenia, integrating genetic, evolutionary, and phenotypic evidence to identify potential protective factors and pathways that could inform future prevention and treatment strategies.
FINDINGS: The review highlights that common genetic variants may confer resilience by enhancing neural plasticity, fluid intelligence, and visual cognition. Candidate protective traits span obstetric, immunological, cognitive, and visual domains, though direct links to specific resilience variants remain unestablished. Evolutionary pressures may have shaped these adaptations to buffer polygenic liability for schizophrenia.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this work synthesizes emerging but preliminary evidence rather than definitive findings. The lack of direct causal links between resilience variants and mechanisms limits conclusions. The evolutionary framing is speculative, and many proposed pathways (e.g., immune or obstetric) require further validation. The discussion of neural plasticity and cognition is plausible but not yet supported by robust empirical data.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This review does not yet change clinical practice but suggests future research directions, such as targeting neural plasticity or cognitive resilience in early intervention strategies. Clinicians should remain cautious about overinterpreting these hypotheses until mechanistic and translational evidence emerges.

item.title: [6] Dynamic gene expression signatures predict psychotherapy response in PTSD.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study investigated whether dynamic, longitudinal changes in gene expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) could predict psychotherapy response in veterans with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). It used a dual-state approach (unstimulated and dexamethasone-stimulated) to assess transcriptional trajectories in PTSD patients (n=17 with complete data) and controls (n=23) at pre-treatment, post-treatment, and follow-up.
FINDINGS: At pre-treatment, unstimulated responders (n=6) and non-responders (n=11) showed pronounced transcriptional differences, exceeding those between PTSD patients and controls. Longitudinally, responders shifted toward control-like gene expression profiles, while non-responders retained persistent divergence. Pathway analyses highlighted Class C/3 G-protein-coupled receptor pathways (e.g., bitter taste receptors, TAS2Rs) and subgroup-specific regulation of GABAB, opioid, and NMDA receptor signaling. Dexamethasone-induced responses further differentiated subgroups, suggesting glucocorticoid sensitivity as a predictor of treatment outcomes.
INTERPRETATION: This is a small, exploratory cohort study (n=17 PTSD patients) without randomization or blinding, limiting causal inference and generalizability. The dynamic dual-state approach is innovative but requires validation in larger, more diverse samples with standardized psychotherapy protocols. The observed transcriptional shifts in responders are intriguing but not yet clinically actionable due to the small sample size and lack of replication. The study highlights potential biomarkers (e.g., TAS2Rs, glucocorticoid sensitivity) but does not establish their predictive utility or mechanistic role in PTSD recovery.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings are preliminary and do not yet change clinical practice. They suggest that dynamic gene expression profiling *might* one day help predict psychotherapy response in PTSD, but further research is needed to confirm these signals and their clinical utility. For now, treatment decisions should rely on established clinical assessments (e.g., CAPS-5) rather than gene expression markers.

item.title: [22] The effectiveness of meaning-based interventions in reducing suicide-related vulnerability: A systematic review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The review asks whether meaning-based interventions (e.g., meaning-centered therapy, dignity therapy) reduce suicide-related vulnerability (ideation, hopelessness, demoralization) and how any benefits are mediated. Ten heterogeneous studies (7 RCTs, 2 quasi-experimental, 1 secondary analysis) were synthesized narratively.
FINDINGS: Across studies, meaning-based interventions consistently improved existential outcomes (meaning in life, spiritual well-being, quality of life) with moderate effect sizes. Emotional outcomes showed mixed and smaller effects. Suicide-related outcomes (hopelessness, demoralization, suicidal ideation) generally decreased, but results varied by population and intervention; no pooled effect sizes were reported.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is small, methodologically mixed, and lacks meta-analytic pooling, limiting certainty. Most studies were at moderate risk of bias; heterogeneity in populations (e.g., advanced cancer, veterans, general psychiatric outpatients) and interventions precludes firm conclusions. The pattern suggests potential benefit via existential pathways, but causal mediation remains unproven. Larger, preregistered RCTs with standardized outcomes and mediation analyses are needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not justify wholesale adoption of meaning-based interventions for suicide prevention outside research settings. Clinicians may consider adjunctive meaning-centered approaches for patients with existential distress, while monitoring suicide-related outcomes closely and integrating with evidence-based treatments.

item.title: [16] Vitamin D Supplementation and Improvement in Insomnia Symptoms Among Malaysian Women With Vitamin D Deficiency: Protocol for a Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Insomnia is common and disabling, and low vitamin D levels may contribute to sleep disturbance, especially in women. This is a double-blind, parallel-group randomized controlled trial (RCT) protocol testing weekly high-dose vitamin D₃ (50 000 IU) versus placebo for 9 weeks in Malaysian women aged 19–50 years with serum 25(OH)D <20 ng/mL and insomnia symptoms.
FINDINGS: Recruitment began December 2023; by July 2026, 42 were screened, 33 enrolled, 22 completed, 4 were still receiving intervention, and 1 withdrew. No efficacy results are yet available because the trial is ongoing and unblinded.
INTERPRETATION: This is a well-designed RCT protocol with clear allocation concealment and validated sleep measures, but no outcome data are available to judge efficacy. The small sample size and single-centre, community-based setting limit generalisability. Until results are published, any claim of benefit remains speculative.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support routine vitamin D supplementation for insomnia. Clinicians should await trial results before considering vitamin D as adjunctive therapy; CBT remains first-line.

item.title: [12] Characterizing Behavioral Engagement in Smartphone Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Obsessive Compulsive Disorder: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This secondary analysis of a 12-week RCT (N=60) examined behavioral engagement in smartphone cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for OCD using 21 objective app analytics variables. It aimed to characterize engagement profiles, link them to OCD symptom change, and explore associations with pretreatment credibility/expectancy and posttreatment satisfaction.
FINDINGS: Cluster analysis identified three engagement profiles: high (35%), moderate (52%), and low (13%) users. All clusters showed significant pre- to posttreatment reductions in OCD severity (Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale), with no significant differences in symptom change across clusters. Cluster 3 (low users) reported lower treatment credibility, expectancy, and satisfaction than cluster 2, while app quality ratings were similar across clusters.
INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates feasibility of multidimensional engagement measurement in digital CBT, but the lack of differential symptom improvement across engagement profiles challenges simplistic dose-response assumptions. The findings may reflect true equivalence in effectiveness across engagement levels or be limited by small sample size and insufficient power to detect meaningful differences. Pretreatment expectations appear linked to engagement patterns, suggesting a modifiable target for improving adherence.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These results imply that even low engagement with smartphone CBT for OCD may yield clinical benefit, though expectations may influence engagement and satisfaction. Clinicians should consider addressing pretreatment expectations to enhance participation, but should not assume higher engagement necessarily leads to better outcomes.

item.title: [12] Mortality Among People With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is associated with increased all-cause and cause-specific mortality and whether ADHD medication modifies this risk. The study included 19 observational studies with over 15 million participants.
FINDINGS: ADHD was associated with increased all-cause mortality (HR 1.71, 95% CI 1.31–2.24), suicide (HR 1.89, 95% CI 1.21–2.95), unintentional or intentional injury (HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.22–2.00), and natural-cause mortality (HR 1.27, 95% CI 1.16–1.38). Among individuals with ADHD, medication use was associated with lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.64–0.87). Substantial heterogeneity was reported across studies.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests ADHD is linked to higher mortality across multiple causes, with medication associated with reduced risk. However, the observational nature of included studies, substantial heterogeneity, and potential confounding limit causal inference. The association between medication and reduced mortality may reflect confounding by indication or severity rather than a direct causal protective effect.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings support timely diagnosis and treatment of ADHD, particularly given the elevated mortality risk. Clinicians should remain vigilant about suicide risk and injury prevention in this population, while recognizing that the protective effect of medication requires further confirmation in robust study designs.

item.title: [9] Concentrated Exposure Therapy vs Internet-Based Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This single-center randomized controlled trial (RCT) compared the efficacy of a concentrated 4-day exposure-based intervention (Bergen 4-day treatment, B4DT) with an 8-week unguided internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy (iCBT) for adults with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), assessing outcomes over 3 months.
FINDINGS: 119 adults (mean age 33.5 years, 66.4% women) were randomized to B4DT (n=60) or iCBT (n=59). At posttreatment, B4DT showed a significantly greater reduction in OCD symptoms (Y-BOCS) than iCBT (mean difference -7.9 points, 95% CI -9.7 to -6.0; Hedges g = -1.6). At 3-month follow-up, the difference remained significant but smaller (mean difference -5.6 points, 95% CI -7.8 to -3.4; Hedges g = -1.0). Response and remission rates at follow-up were higher with B4DT (61.4% vs 25.0% and 42.1% vs 13.6%, respectively).
INTERPRETATION: The study provides high-quality RCT evidence that B4DT is superior to unguided iCBT for OCD symptom reduction, with large effect sizes at posttreatment and moderate effects sustained at 3 months. Strengths include masked outcome assessment, intention-to-treat analysis, and clear superiority in both primary and secondary outcomes. However, the single-center design, predominantly female sample, and lack of active iCBT comparator (e.g., therapist-guided) limit generalizability. The concentrated format may improve access but requires replication in diverse settings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: B4DT may offer a more effective and time-efficient alternative to unguided iCBT for OCD, particularly where rapid symptom reduction is prioritized. Clinicians should consider patient preferences and logistical constraints when choosing between formats, while awaiting broader validation.

item.title: [7] Home Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation With Gamified Cognitive Control Training for Depression: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This multicenter, double-masked randomized clinical trial (RCT) evaluated the feasibility, safety, and efficacy of home-based transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) combined with gamified cognitive control training (CCT) versus sham tDCS plus sham game in adults (18–65 years) with major depressive disorder (MDD). The study addressed whether this combined home-based approach could improve depressive symptoms more than sham treatment.
FINDINGS: Of 111 enrolled participants, 109 were included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (55 active, 54 sham). Feasibility was met, with 78.9% (lower bound of 1-sided 95% CI, 71.5%) completing ≥20 of 30 sessions. Both groups showed MADRS score improvements at week 6, with no significant difference between groups (difference: 0.89 [95% CI, -1.37 to 3.15]; P = .44; Cohen d = 0.10 [95% CI, -0.15 to 0.34]). Results were consistent at week 10 follow-up. Adverse events were balanced between groups.
INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates that home-based tDCS with CCT is feasible and safe, but it does not show superior efficacy to sham treatment for reducing depressive symptoms in MDD. The small effect size (Cohen d = 0.10) suggests no clinically meaningful difference. Limitations include the lack of an active comparator (e.g., standard tDCS alone) and potential expectancy effects despite masking checks. The population was relatively young and predominantly female, which may limit generalizability. Further research is needed to optimize the combination of tDCS and behavioral interventions.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support the use of home-based tDCS combined with gamified CCT as a superior treatment for MDD over sham. Clinicians should remain cautious about adopting this approach until more robust evidence emerges. Further trials should explore optimal stimulation parameters and cognitive interventions.

item.title: [7] Assessing the Impact of Metacognitive Therapy on OCD Severity and Beliefs: A Three-Wave Multisite RCT With Panel Mediation Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This assessor-blinded multisite RCT (n=76 adults with OCD in Pakistan) tested whether 12 weekly sessions of individual metacognitive therapy (MCT) reduce OCD severity more than treatment-as-usual (TAU) and whether changes in metacognitive beliefs temporally precede symptom improvement.
FINDINGS: MCT produced greater reductions in clinician-rated Y-BOCS severity than TAU (F(1.81, 134)=11.30, p<0.001), with mean differences of −4.00 at post-treatment and −6.92 at 6-month follow-up (both p<0.001). MCT also reduced Metacognitions Questionnaire-30 belief domains, maintained at follow-up. However, the prespecified lagged indirect effect through post-treatment beliefs was not supported (β=−0.01).
INTERPRETATION: The trial shows MCT outperforms TAU for OCD severity with moderate-to-large effects at post-treatment and follow-up, supporting external validity in a non-Western outpatient setting. However, the lack of temporal precedence in the mediation analysis weakens claims that metacognitive belief change is a causal mechanism. Limitations include small sample size, single-blind assessment, and absence of active comparator (e.g., ERP), leaving uncertainty about MCT’s superiority to established treatments. Funding sources are not reported.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: MCT may be a viable alternative where ERP is declined or unavailable, but clinicians should note that the mechanism remains unclear and comparative effectiveness against first-line treatments is untested.

item.title: [6] Structural network alterations and peripheral immune-inflammatory dysregulation define distinct subtypes of major depressive disorder with prognostic implications.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This study investigated whether immune-inflammatory dysregulation and cortical structural changes in major depressive disorder (MDD) interact systematically, and whether they define clinically meaningful subtypes. It combined genome-wide association data with a prospective cohort of 122 MDD patients and 66 healthy controls who underwent MRI and immune marker assessments.
FINDINGS: Genetically predicted MDD was linked to lower circulating IGF-1 (pFDR = 0.013). Higher IL-5 and leptin levels correlated with reduced gray matter volume in the right cingulate gyrus and bilateral putamen (pFDR < 0.05). Structural covariance network analysis identified two subtypes: hypoconnectivity (n = 49) with greater anxiety and anhedonia, and hyperconnectivity (n = 73) with elevated inflammatory markers and faster antidepressant response (p = 0.032).
INTERPRETATION: The study provides preliminary evidence for immune-brain interaction in MDD and suggests two neurobiological subtypes with distinct symptom profiles and treatment responses. However, the sample size is modest, follow-up is short, and causality cannot be inferred from associations. The clinical relevance of subtype-specific immune markers and the stability of subtypes over time remain uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings do not yet justify subtype-specific treatment choices but suggest that immune profiling and network connectivity measures might eventually help personalize MDD care. Further validation in larger, longer studies is needed before bedside application.

item.title: [6] Greater proximity to greenspace is associated with fewer depressive symptoms among urban middle-aged adults.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This observational cohort study used machine-learning (Support Vector Machines) to rank predictors of depressive symptoms among 1,542 urban middle-aged adults in China, asking whether residential greenspace proximity matters more than other health and social factors.
FINDINGS: The best-performing model (AUC 0.776) identified life satisfaction, greenspace (EVI250 m), social activity, pain, sleep duration and instrumental-ADL impairment as significant predictors. Closer greenspace exposure was associated with fewer depressive symptoms; Shapley values placed greenspace among the top influential factors.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s internal validity is limited by its cross-sectional design and reliance on satellite-derived greenspace metrics rather than direct environmental measurements. The ML approach improves variable ranking but cannot establish causality or rule out residual confounding (e.g., unmeasured neighbourhood or lifestyle factors). The reported AUC suggests moderate predictive power, but effect sizes for greenspace proximity are not provided, so clinical significance remains uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings suggest that urban greenspace may be a relevant—but likely modest—contributor to mental health; they do not yet justify changing practice, but they support further longitudinal and interventional research.

item.title: [15] Dual benefit of esketamine-based opioid-free anesthesia on postoperative pain and mental health outcomes in patients undergoing bariatric surgery: a randomized controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This double-blind randomized controlled trial (RCT) investigated whether esketamine-based opioid-free anesthesia (OFA) improves postoperative pain and 3-month mental health outcomes in morbidly obese patients undergoing laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy, compared to conventional opioid-based anesthesia.
FINDINGS: 84 patients were randomized (1:1) to esketamine-based OFA (n=42) or opioid-based anesthesia with remifentanil (n=42). 74 (88.1%) completed 3-month follow-up. Postoperative pain intensity within 24 hours was significantly lower in the esketamine group (P < 0.01), with fewer patients experiencing moderate-to-severe pain (P < 0.05). At 3 months, mental health outcomes were significantly better in the esketamine group. Adverse events did not differ significantly between groups. Pharmacokinetic analysis confirmed rapid esketamine metabolism to active (S)-norketamine.
INTERPRETATION: The study suggests esketamine-based OFA may offer dual benefits for acute pain and longer-term mental health without increasing adverse events. Strengths include the double-blind RCT design, clear co-primary outcomes, and pharmacokinetic confirmation. However, the sample size is modest, follow-up is limited to 3 months, and the mental health assessment tools are not specified. The lack of blinding details for outcome assessors and potential unmeasured confounders (e.g., baseline mental health severity) limit certainty. The clinical significance of the observed mental health improvement remains uncertain given the short follow-up and unspecified measures.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Esketamine-based OFA may be a promising alternative to opioid-based anesthesia in bariatric surgery, potentially improving immediate postoperative pain and 3-month mental health outcomes. However, larger trials with longer follow-up and validated mental health measures are needed before recommending a change in practice.

item.title: [14] Impact of clozapine on the proteome: A systematic review and functional analyses.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS), but its use is limited by serious adverse effects. This systematic review and functional proteomic analysis aimed to integrate proteomic findings associated with clozapine exposure across animal, human, and cell-based models to better understand its mechanisms and potential biomarkers.
FINDINGS: Across 1070 unique proteins altered by clozapine (603 increased, 394 decreased, 73 discordant), 152 were identified in ≥2 studies, with 79 showing concordant directionality. Nine proteins were replicated in ≥3 studies. STRING pathway analysis revealed recurrent enrichment in immune/inflammatory, cellular-stress, and neuronal pathways, with stratified analyses supporting these and related metabolic processes. IPA highlighted necrosis-related processes and downstream effects in cardiovascular, hepatic, and renal systems. No direct comparison of brain and peripheral blood changes was available.
INTERPRETATION: This systematic review provides preliminary evidence that clozapine may influence immune, inflammatory, and cell-death pathways, potentially contributing to adverse effects. However, the evidence is heterogeneous, with limited replication of specific proteins and no direct clinical correlation to treatment response or adverse outcomes. The lack of longitudinal human data and time-series comparisons limits causal inference. The findings are hypothesis-generating and underscore the need for prospective proteomic studies during clozapine initiation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current proteomic data do not yet translate to clinical practice but suggest potential biomarkers for monitoring clozapine-related adverse effects. Clinicians should remain vigilant for immune-mediated complications (e.g., myocarditis) but should not alter prescribing based on these findings alone. Further research is needed to validate these pathways as therapeutic targets or biomarkers.

item.title: [12] Harm reduction among refugees and displaced populations in Lebanon: a systematic review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review (PRISMA; PROSPERO-registered) examined harm reduction policies and services for substance use among refugees and displaced populations in Lebanon, a setting with high refugee density and complex legal/healthcare barriers. The review aimed to map service availability, access barriers, and policy gaps to guide interventions.
FINDINGS: Out of 387 records, 29 documents (17 peer-reviewed studies and 12 grey literature reports) were included. No structured harm reduction policies specifically for refugees were identified. Key barriers included legal restrictions, stigma, and poor integration of harm reduction into routine care. Only 4 of 12 grey literature sources mentioned harm reduction provision, and none outlined a comprehensive strategy. Many studies were broad and lacked focused substance-use data in refugee populations.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is weak and fragmented, with high risk of selection and reporting biases due to reliance on grey literature and heterogeneous, often non-refugee-specific studies. The Joanna Briggs Institute tool was used for risk-of-bias assessment, but the overall quality of included evidence appears low. The lack of policy specificity and integrated services is clear, but causal pathways and effect sizes remain unquantified. Further targeted research is essential to inform policy adaptation and service design.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current harm reduction services in Lebanon do not adequately address refugee needs; clinicians should anticipate gaps in access and advocate for mobile clinics and integrated HCV screening. However, evidence to guide specific clinical interventions is currently insufficient.

item.title: [11] Brain functional changes of suicidal ideation and behaviours: a meta-analysis of task-based fMRI studies.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This pre-registered meta-analysis of 22 task-based fMRI studies examined brain functional changes associated with suicidal ideation and behaviours, comparing 459 suicidal individuals with 681 non-suicidal psychiatric controls. The study aimed to clarify neural underpinnings of suicidality amid methodological heterogeneity.
FINDINGS: In emotion tasks, general suicidality and suicidal behaviours were linked to hyperactivity in the left sensorimotor cortices and hippocampus/parahippocampus, alongside hypoactivity in bilateral visual cortices. Only the visual cortex hypoactivity was consistently replicated across all subgroup analyses. In non-emotion tasks, hyperactivity in the left precentral gyrus and right middle temporal gyrus was observed for general suicidality and suicidal behaviours, consistently replicated across subgroups. Meta-regression showed larger functional changes in frontotemporal regions with higher female proportions and in hippocampal/temporal regions with older participants.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is moderate in strength due to methodological heterogeneity across studies (e.g., varied diagnoses, task types). The consistent finding of visual cortex hypoactivity in emotion tasks and motor/temporal hyperactivity in non-emotion tasks suggests potential neural targets for intervention. However, the clinical significance of these neural changes remains uncertain, as effect sizes and direct clinical outcomes were not reported. The study’s reliance on task-based fMRI and subgroup analyses limits generalisability to routine psychiatric care.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings highlight potential neural correlates of suicidality but do not yet translate into actionable clinical tools. Further research is needed to determine if these neural patterns can guide treatment or risk assessment in psychiatric practice.

item.title: [9] Targeting affective cognition during pregnancy to prevent postpartum depression: a randomized controlled trial with parity-specific effects.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This randomized controlled trial (RCT) tested whether prenatal affective cognitive training (PACT) reduces postpartum depression (PPD) risk in pregnant women at heightened risk by targeting negative cognitive biases related to infant cues. The study included 147 pregnant women identified as high-risk, randomized to PACT or care as usual (CAU), with outcomes assessed up to six months postpartum.
FINDINGS: The primary outcome, PPD incidence within six months postpartum, did not differ significantly between PACT (14%) and CAU (24%) overall (p = 0.18). Secondary outcomes, including depressive symptoms over the first six weeks postpartum, also showed no significant difference (p = 0.31). However, PACT significantly improved positive interpretation of infant emotions post-intervention (p = 0.003). Exploratory analyses revealed a markedly lower PPD incidence in multiparous women receiving PACT (5%) compared to CAU (35%), with an odds ratio of 0.10 (95% CI [0.01-0.92], p = 0.04). Follow-up data were available for 83% of participants.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s internal validity is strengthened by its RCT design and structured intervention, but the lack of overall effect on PPD incidence limits conclusions. The significant improvement in affective cognition suggests the intervention may target relevant mechanisms, though clinical significance is unclear. The exploratory parity-specific findings are intriguing but require cautious interpretation due to small subgroup sizes and lack of correction for multiple testing. The high dropout-adjusted follow-up rate (83%) is a strength, but the study’s power may have been insufficient for subgroup analyses. External validity is limited by the selective high-risk population and single-center setting.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: PACT does not currently reduce PPD risk overall, so it cannot be recommended for routine practice. However, the parity-specific effect in multiparous women warrants further investigation in larger, adequately powered trials to determine if targeted interventions could benefit specific subgroups. Clinicians should remain cautious about overinterpreting exploratory findings.

item.title: [9] Structure based discovery of antipsychotic-like TAAR1 agonists.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This preclinical study used computational docking and experimental screening to discover novel trace amine-associated receptor 1 (TAAR1) agonists as potential antipsychotic agents in schizophrenia, where current dopamine/serotonin-targeting treatments have limited efficacy and side effects.
FINDINGS: From 65 million computationally screened molecules, 55 were experimentally tested, yielding 14 TAAR1 agonists with mid-nanomolar to micromolar potencies. Hit optimization produced nanomolar agonists, with three compounds demonstrating high brain exposure and potency comparable to or exceeding the investigational drug ulotaront. All three normalized amphetamine-induced pre-pulse inhibition in mice (a schizophrenia model) without inducing catalepsy, a common side effect of traditional antipsychotics.
INTERPRETATION: This is a high-throughput, computational-experimental drug discovery study with strong internal validity in its methodology (docking, cryo-EM confirmation, behavioral assays). However, it is entirely preclinical, conducted in mice, and lacks human data. The functional selectivity and lack of catalepsy are promising, but clinical relevance remains uncertain until safety and efficacy are tested in humans. The risk of over-optimization for initial hit rates is noted but not quantified.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No immediate change to clinical practice is warranted. These findings justify further development and human trials but should not alter current antipsychotic prescribing.

item.title: [9] Effect of a Subanesthetic Dose of Esketamine on Postoperative Sleep Disturbance After Oocyte Retrieval Under Intravenous Anesthesia: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=196) tested whether a single subanesthetic dose of esketamine (0.2 mg/kg IV) reduces postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD) on day 3 after oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia in women.
FINDINGS: In intention-to-treat analysis, PSD incidence on POD 3 was 13.06% with esketamine vs 24.90% with placebo (risk difference −11.84 pp [95% CI −22.98 to −0.69]; RR 0.52 [95% CI 0.28–0.99]; P=0.047). Per-protocol results were similar. PSD on POD 1 did not differ. Postoperative pain at 30 min was lower with esketamine (P<0.001), but dreaming was more frequent (21.4% vs 11.2%; P=0.048) and recovery metrics were modestly longer (time to alertness 12 vs 11 min; PACU stay 34 vs 31 min; both P≤0.005).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests a modest reduction in PSD at POD 3 with esketamine, but the effect size is small (RR ~0.5) and the confidence interval barely excludes the null. The trial is single-center, short-term, and lacks long-term sleep or functional outcomes. Recovery time and dreaming frequency are slightly increased.
